title: A push becomes a turn
question: A piston slides. A wheel turns. What links them?
idea: An engine uses energy to make motion. Let's follow a push through its parts.

motion.title: Follow the push

steps.label: Fuel burns
steps.text: Fuel stores energy. It burns with air inside the engine. The gases get hot.

steps.label: Gases push
steps.text: The hot gases spread out. They push the piston along its tube.

steps.label: A shaft turns
steps.text: The rod links the piston to the crankshaft. One push turns the shaft partway.

motion.caption: A simple parts picture. More pushes help keep the shaft turning. Other parts carry the turn to the wheels.
motion.gesture: Slide one hand back and forth like a piston. Make a circle with your other hand. Two kinds of motion!

math.title: How far to 60?
math.parentNote: 3 min: trace the parts and count by 2. 9 min: solve with tens and ones or jumps. 3 min: explain a strategy. If stuck, ask: How far to the next ten? These are pretend counts, not engine speeds.
math.intro: The crankshaft turns. One turn goes all the way around. Help Jo count a model engine's turns.
tasks: Jo counts 24 turns, then 18 more. How many turns in all? Draw jumps or tens and ones.
Jo wants to reach 60 turns. The count is 42. How many more turns? Show your thinking.
Count by 2. Say each number. Fill the empty spaces.
math.extension: Tell Jo: How can adding help you check your subtraction?
hints: Try counting up from 42 to 50, then to 60.

reading.title: The push inside
reading.parentNote: 3 min: preview the words. 7 min: read together, then reread. 5 min: discuss both questions. Help with piston and crankshaft. Ask: Which words helped you? Pointing and spoken answers count.
paragraphs: Jo gives a toy car a push. Its wheels turn. “Who pushes inside a real car?” asks Leo.
They look at a picture of a gasoline engine. Fuel stores energy. Inside the engine, fuel burns with air. The gases get hot.
The hot gases spread out. They push a part called a piston. It slides back and forth inside a tube.
A rod links the piston to a crankshaft. The piston slides. The rod moves. The crankshaft turns! Other parts carry the turn to the wheels.
“A push becomes a turn!” says Leo. The engine changes some of the fuel's energy into motion. Some energy warms the engine and the air.

words.meaning: what can make things move or change
a part that slides inside a tube
a turning shaft linked to the piston by a rod

questions: What pushes the piston? Point to or underline the words that tell you.
Which part slides? Which part turns? Tell how the rod links them.

check.prompt: Leo says, “The fuel pushes the wheels.” What would you tell him?
choices: The gases push a piston. Parts carry the motion.
feedback: Look at the middle of the story. The gases push a piston. Follow the rod to the turning shaft. Try again.
You followed the parts! Hot gases push the piston. The rod links it to the crankshaft. Other parts carry the turn to the wheels.

writing.title: Pass the wonder on
writing.parentNote: 3 min: say the steps aloud. 4 min: draw and label. 6 min: write 3 short sentences. 2 min: reread. Use the frames if helpful. Accept invented spelling or write the child's spoken words.
writing.intro: Teach a friend how a gasoline engine makes motion. Say it, draw it, then write 3 short sentences.
writing.draw: Draw the piston, rod, and crankshaft. Label them. Add a straight arrow and a curved arrow.

frames.hint: What turning part does it link to?

writing.check: Read it to a friend. Can they follow the push to the turn? Check a capital and an end mark in each sentence.

answers.label: Math · 1
answers.text: 42 turns. Add 10, then 8: 24 → 34 → 42. Or combine 3 tens and 12 ones; trade 10 ones for a ten to get 4 tens and 2 ones. Ask the child to explain a jump or a trade.

answers.label: Math · 2
answers.text: 18 more turns. Count up: 42 + 8 = 50; 50 + 10 = 60. The two jumps total 18. Check: 42 + 18 = 60, so 60 - 42 = 18. Accept any sound strategy.

answers.label: Math · 3
answers.text: Missing numbers: 6, 8, 12, 16, 20. Each step adds 2. Ask: How many pairs make 10? (5.) The digital counter groups turns in pairs; it does not count piston pushes or measure fuel use.

answers.label: Reading · 1
answers.text: Hot gases. Evidence: “The hot gases spread out. They push a part called a piston.” If the child says fuel, reread these two sentences together. Fuel burns with air; the gases push the piston.

answers.label: Reading · 2
answers.text: The piston slides; the crankshaft turns. The rod links them. Other parts carry the turn to the wheels. For Leo's digital question, choose the answer about gases and a piston. Invite the child to trace the parts.

answers.label: Writing
answers.text: Example: “First, fuel burns with air. Next, hot gases push the piston. Then, the rod links it to the turning crankshaft.” Look for a clear sequence, labels, and straight/curved motion arrows. Praise the explanation before helping with capitals or end marks.

parentGuidance: This is one kind of engine: a gasoline piston engine. Electric cars use motors powered by electricity. The picture shows part of a stroke, not a full engine cycle; one push is not one full turn. The crankshaft also moves the piston through the rod. Valves, timing, and drivetrain parts are omitted. Use pictures, gestures, or a toy car, not real engines or fuel. Pause between the three sessions.
